content_blocks.title: Know Your Enemy, Know Yourself
content_blocks.content: Threat modeling isn't about fear — it's about focus. Without it, you're defending everything equally, which means you're defending nothing well. Understanding who targets your industry, how they operate, and what they want lets you invest where it matters. It's the difference between bolting every door and guarding the one the burglar will actually use.

content_blocks.title: Threat Modeling Methodologies
content_blocks.content: **STRIDE** (Microsoft) categorizes threats by type: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. It's systematic but doesn't inherently prioritize. **PASTA** (Risk Centric) aligns threats to business objectives across 7 stages: from defining assets through attack modeling to risk analysis. **Diamond Model** maps the adversarial relationship: Adversary ↔ Capability ↔ Infrastructure ↔ Victim. Choose STRIDE for system-level analysis, PASTA for business-aligned risk, Diamond for threat actor tracking.

content_blocks.title: Teach Me Like I'm 10: Threat Modeling
content_blocks.content: Think of your house. A threat model asks: Who might break in? (Burglars? Kids sneaking out?) How would they do it? (Through the window? The back door?) What would they steal? (TV? Jewelry?) And what can I do about it? (Alarm system? Better locks?) Threat modeling is just asking these questions about your digital house, but with frameworks that make sure you don't forget any doors or windows.

content_blocks.title: STRIDE Analysis Template
content_blocks.content:
```markdown
# STRIDE Threat Model: [System Name]

## System Boundary
- **Asset:** [What we're protecting]
- **Trust Level:** [User, Admin, System]
- **Entry Points:** [APIs, UI, Network]

## Threat Analysis
| STRIDE Category | Threat Scenario | Affected Asset | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spoofing | Attacker forges API token | User API | OAuth2 + mTLS |
| Tampering | Modified config in transit | Config store | Integrity checks |
| Repudiation | User denies destructive action | Audit logs | Immutable logging |
| Info Disclosure | PII in error messages | User data | Sanitization layer |
| DoS | API rate limit bypass | API gateway | Rate limiting |
| Elevation | Regular user gains admin | RBAC system | Role validation |
```

content_blocks.title: Real-World: Threat Actor Profiling Drives Priorities
content_blocks.content: A healthcare organization models threats and discovers: financially motivated ransomware operators (FIN7, Clop) target their sector most frequently, while nation-state actors (APT41) target medical research. The tactical intel (IOCs, TTPs) tells the SOC what to detect. The operational intel (campaign timelines, infrastructure churn) tells IR when to be on high alert. The strategic intel (shift from data theft to ransomware) tells the CISO where to invest budget. Each level serves a different decision-maker.

content_blocks.title: Threat Intelligence Levels: SOT
content_blocks.content:
**SOT** — the three levels of threat intelligence:
- **S**trategic — Who and Why (threat actor motivations, sector trends, geopolitical context)
- **O**perational — When and Where (campaign timelines, infrastructure, targeting patterns)
- **T**actical — What and How (IOCs, hashes, domains, specific TTPs)

Strategic informs leadership. Operational informs defenders. Tactical informs detectors.

content_blocks.title: Build a Threat Model
content_blocks.content:
Your organization is a fintech startup with a web application, mobile app, and AWS backend:
1. Using STRIDE, identify the top 2 threats per category
2. Which threat actor type is most likely to target you? Why?
3. Map one strategic, one operational, and one tactical intelligence need
4. What single security investment would reduce the most risk?

Write your answers before moving on.

content_blocks.title: Threat Modeling Is Iterative
content_blocks.content: Your first threat model will be wrong — and that's fine. The value isn't perfection; it's structured thinking. Update it when you get new intelligence, after incidents, and when your architecture changes. A threat model that's never updated is worse than no threat model — it creates false confidence. Treat it as a living document.
